task:
Write today's learning-log note for me.

Today is 25 November 2026. "Recent" means published after August 2026. Don't put a year in search queries unless a source
gave it to you, and take every date in the note from a source, never from memory.

1. Pick ONE specific, recent development in one of these areas: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); evaluating LLM applications; Model Context Protocol (MCP); running small language models on a CPU.
   Not something earlier notes covered. Earlier notes: Hand‑Optimized q1_0 Dot Product Boosts Llama.cpp CPU Inference (June 2024); Adaptive Neural Reranking Boosts RAG Accuracy (2026).
2. Research it: search, then read at least two different sources (web_read) to check the facts. Searches look at
   primary sources first (papers, code, official docs and blogs); prefer those over secondary write-ups.
   Pick something concrete: a paper, a release, a spec change, a tool, not a general trend.
3. Call write_note exactly once, with a specific title (not "Recent advances in RAG") and a markdown body
   with these sections:
   ## What happened   (2-4 sentences)
   ## Why it matters for my projects   (I build RAG, LLM evaluation, MCP servers and small LLMs on a CPU laptop)
   ## Key details   (3-6 bullet points, each with its [n] citation)
   ## Try it   (one small concrete thing I could try, if there is one)
   Under 350 words. Cite only sources you read. Don't add a Sources section: it's added automatically.
4. Then reply with one line: the title.

{
 "n": 3,
 "title": "A More Predictable Release Cycle for MCP | Model Context Protocol Blog",
 "url": "https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/mcp-release-cycle",
 "text": "We’ve spent a lot of time over the past two years talking about ways to improve MCP, add new features and capabilities, and get on a more predictable release cadence. Clearly, there has been no shortage of ideas both from the maintainer and broader developer community. Getting those ideas reviewed, implemented, tested, and into a release is a whole other part of the job, and we want to make that specific part easier to follow for our community.

For folks working on proposals, that means knowing when reviews will happen and how much time there is to make adjustments. SDK maintainers also need to know when the spec will stop changing - both client and server developers use our developer toolchain as a starting point to try new MCP capabilities out and share feedback. To make this process easier, we’re setting up a more consistent timeline for upcoming spec changes so that you don’t have to piece a schedule together from meeting notes and GitHub threads.

The Core Maintainers worked through these questions together at MCPCon Europe, and Kurtis Van Gent recently wrote up the process in SEP-3398: Release Cycle Updates - this is our de facto release guidance moving forward.

As a result of this work, we’re moving MCP specification releases to a regular six-month schedule.

[...]

For the next release, we’re targeting March 30, 2027 - expect MCP version 2027-03-30 to land then.

To keep that schedule predictable, a proposal that isn’t ready will move to a later release rather than delay the whole spec. Its authors can keep working on it without having to rush, and everyone else can continue preparing for the release they planned around.

## Introducing the Release Manager role#

[...]

We’ll be working with proposal authors and SDK maintainers throughout the cycle, and Luca Chang will join David and myself as a Release Manager for the next specification cycle.

[...]

Eight months before release: planning begins. We gather feedback from maintainers and Working Groups about what to work on and what depends on what.

Six months before release: Core Maintainer reviews begin and run until soft freeze.

[...]

One and a half months before release: Tier 1 SDK betas arrive with support for the frozen specification.

[...]

Lastly, when SDK betas are available, we’d love for the broader MCP community to try them with the clients and servers they already run. This is a great opportunity to catch any last-minute issues and gives the maintainers time to work through any reported bugs or inconsistencies while corrections can still go into the release.

If you have an idea for improving MCP, we encourage you to bring it to a Working Group and help shape it with other contributors. You don’t need a finished proposal to join the conversation, and you most certainly don’t need to wait for the next release cycle.

[...]

If you’ve been thinking about contributing to the protocol, come chat with us - we’d love your help!",

{"body":"## What happened
On 28 July 2026 the Model Context Protocol (MCP) released a new specification version, 2026‑07‑28. The update formalized a shift to a stateless, extension‑driven protocol and deprecated legacy features such as Roots, Sampling, and Logging. It also announced a new six‑month release cadence, with the next version slated for 30 March 2027, and introduced a Release Manager role to streamline proposals and SDK betas.

## Why it matters for my projects
Your RAG pipelines, LLM evaluation tools, MCP servers, and CPU‑based small LLMs all rely on consistent protocol behavior. The 2026‑07‑28 spec gives you a stable target for client and server development, removes deprecated paths that could break backward compatibility, and provides a predictable schedule for future changes—critical for planning feature rollouts and testing.

## Key details
- MCP 2026‑07‑28 is the current specification, using date‑based versioning and emphasizing stateless requests and an Extensions framework. [1]
- Legacy concepts (Roots, Sampling, Logging) are deprecated, simplifying the protocol surface. [1]
- A six‑month release cycle has been adopted, with the next release on 30 March 2027, to improve predictability for developers. [3]
- A Release Manager role has been added to coordinate proposal reviews, SDK betas, and community feedback. [3]
- The specification update is reflected in the MCP‑gateway‑registry 1.37.0 release notes, which align server implementations with the new spec. [2]

## Try it
Clone the MCP‑gateway‑registry 1.37.0 repository, run the provided integration tests against a 2026‑07‑28 client, and verify that deprecated endpoints (e.g., `/roots`) return the expected deprecation errors. This will confirm your environment is aligned with the latest spec and expose any compatibility gaps in your RAG or evaluation pipelines.
","title":"MCP 2026‑07‑28 Specification Release and Six‑Month Cadence"}

 "text": "This repository contains an implementation of the official Go software

The

servers.

The
github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/jsonrpc package is for users implementing
their own transports.

The
github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/auth
package provides some primitives for supporting OAuth.

The
github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/oauthex
package provides extensions to the OAuth protocol, such as ProtectedResourceMetadata.

The SDK endeavors to implement the full MCP spec. The docs/ directory
contains feature documentation, mapping the MCP spec to the packages above.

The following table shows which versions of the Go SDK support which versions of the MCP specification:

[...]

The roots, sampling, and logging features are deprecated as of protocol version
2026-07-28 by

The SDK continues to support them for compatibility during the deprecation
window (at least twelve months). See the individual feature documentation for
migration guidance.
